items.question: Why can a service become overloaded while rejecting most incoming requests?

section_new.excerpt: ## The overload boundary The overload scenario offers 30 requests per second to a 24-request-per-second pool with a 40-request queue and a one-second deadline. The run reports: - success rate 0.6488 (95% CI 0.6443-0.6534); - timeout rate 0.3495 (95% CI 0.3451-0.3540); - rejection rate 0.0005; - mean queue length 12.79; - server utilization 0.9966. The dominant failure is timeout, not rejection. The queue is large enough to absorb arrivals but not large enough to prevent deadline expiry. A report that focuses on rejection alone would miss most of the loss: rejection is 0.05% while timeout is 35.0%.
section_new.heading: The overload boundary

items.question: What extra recovery coordination can a continuously reconciling GitOps controller require during an emergency rollback?

section_new.excerpt: ## 1. GitOps reconciles desired configuration, not business outcomes A GitOps controller observes versioned desired deployment state and tries to align cluster/runtime resources with it. A clean diff or converged resource state does not mean downstream effects, durable writes or API contracts are correct. Separate: - **source/build artifact identity**: which immutable bytes were tested and approved; - **deployment state**: which revision and configuration an authorized controller attempts to apply; - **runtime readiness**: which instances are ready to accept some work; - **traffic exposure**: which eligible requests reach old or candidate version; - **user outcome**: correctly completed effe
section_new.heading: 1. GitOps reconciles desired configuration, not business outcomes
